title: Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King (2025 TCC)
subject: SR&ED dispute reviewing whether oilfield service projects had sufficient contemporaneous documentation and technological uncertainty.
summary: In Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King (2025 TCC 63), the Tax Court of Canada dismissed a fracking-equipment corporation's SR&ED appeals concerning $1,454,874 (2014) and $507,989 (2015) of claimed expenditures for mobile direct-contact water heaters. Lacking expert evidence, testable hypotheses and contemporaneous records, the claimant failed the Northwest Hydraulic test, confirming that trial and error alone is not SR&ED.
metaDescription: Explore the 2025 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision in Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King and its impact on Canadian R&D claims.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Case Background
1.1 Factual Matrix and the Taxpayer's SR&ED Claim

In Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King, 2025 TCC 63 (Dockets 2019-894(IT)G and 2021-1471(IT)G), the Tax Court of Canada addressed the recurring tension between commercial product engineering and statutorily eligible experimental development under the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program. The Appellant, Vortex Energy Services Ltd., was a Canadian corporation owned equally by four 25% shareholders, including Mr. Andrew Bodner, his father-in-law (an agribusiness operator in the grain sector), and Mr. Joe Bazley. During its 2014 and 2015 taxation years, the Appellant undertook a commercial engineering project aimed at designing and building high-efficiency, direct-contact water heaters capable of being mounted on a truck or trailer to service the hydraulic fracturing ("fracking") industry in Western Canada.

The technical architecture of the Appellant's equipment relied on direct-contact heat transfer, wherein combustion gases generated by a high-capacity burner flowed upward through internal packing material to heat water cascading directly through the vessel. Across the relevant period, the Appellant fabricated and tested three distinct units: Unit 1 and Unit 2, each rated at a thermal output of 10 million British Thermal Units (BTU) per hour, and Unit 3, a scaled-up single unit rated at 35 million BTU per hour. Most of the technical activities during the 2015 taxation year centered on Unit 3.

As the Appellant attempted to scale thermal capacity and optimize combustion within the confined geometry of a mobile, trailer-mounted vessel, it encountered operational difficulties involving internal air pressures, burner sizing, flame geometry, and severe acoustic harmonics. Specifically, enlarging the burner flame inside the vessel induced harmonic disturbances ("rumbles") that subjected the unit's walls and corners to intense mechanical vibration and structural stress, ultimately causing the vessel to leak and, in the case of Unit 1, to shake itself apart and fail catastrophically during testing. To resolve these operational failures, the Appellant—working through Mr. Bodner and various subcontractors—modified the air inlet configuration and altered the burner hole patterns during field testing conducted at Mr. Bazley's cattle farm, including a documented series of trials on April 8, 2014. The Appellant claimed SR&ED expenditures of $1,454,874 for its 2014 taxation year and $507,989 for its 2015 taxation year; after the 2015 expenditures were disallowed, the Appellant did not object but instead carried them forward into its 2019 taxation year, which is why the appeals concern the assessments of its 2014 and 2019 taxation years.
1.2 The Minister's Challenge and Administrative Posture

Upon review and assessment, the Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister"), acting through the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), disallowed the claimed 2014 and 2015 SR&ED expenditures in their entirety and, in reassessing the Appellant's 2019 taxation year, disallowed the carry-forward of the 2015 expenditures. The Crown's central position was that the design, fabrication, and troubleshooting of Units 1, 2, and 3 did not constitute "experimental development" within the meaning of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (Canada) (the "ITA").

By amendments to its Replies granted at the commencement of the hearing, the Crown pleaded the Minister's assumptions that no scientific or technological uncertainty existed, that the Appellant did not formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty, and that its overall approach was not undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or technological advancement; the Minister had also assumed, among other things, that the burner and heater-box modifications rested on existing chemical and mechanical engineering knowledge and that the contractors' expertise was sufficient for the spray-nozzle and software work. Furthermore, the Minister assumed that the Appellant's overall approach was not consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis, an approach the Court ultimately characterized as trial and error. From an evidentiary standpoint, the Appellant did not lead any expert evidence; the Court allowed the CRA reviewer called by the Crown to testify only to place the SR&ED applications in the record and explain how they were reviewed, not to opine on whether the work qualified, excluded as hearsay Mr. Bodner's account of a subcontractor's views, and held that the Appellant's written argument, by relying on evidence excluded at trial, was an impermissible attempt to put expert evidence in "through the back door".
1.3 Governing Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework in Canada

The statutory foundation for Canadian R&D tax incentives rests upon a tripartite structure within the ITA: the threshold definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1), the expenditure deduction and pool carry-forward mechanics in section 37, and the ITC computation and carry-forward provisions in section 127, read in conjunction with Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations. Claimants are statutorily required to file prescribed technical and financial information on Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) and claim the resulting corporate ITCs on Schedule T2SCH31 within the strict 18-month statutory filing deadline following the end of the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred.

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, "scientific research and experimental development" is defined as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". For commercial engineering claimants, eligibility almost universally hinges on paragraph (c) of that definition—namely, "experimental development," which encompasses work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Explicit statutory exclusions under paragraphs (e) through (k) of the definition remove routine data collection, commercial production, style changes, market research, quality control, or routine testing from eligibility.

To operationalize the statutory language of subsection 248(1), Canadian jurisprudence relies universally on the five-criterion sequential test formulated by Judge Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC), and endorsed and applied by the Federal Court of Appeal on several occasions, most recently in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72, where Justice Rennie confirmed that the criteria reflect the court's understanding of what Parliament intended by subsection 248(1). As applied by Justice David E. Spiro in Vortex Energy, a taxpayer bears the legal burden of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, an affirmative answer to all five cumulative questions. First, the claimant must prove there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Second, the claimant must demonstrate that it formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the claimant must show that the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Fourth, the process must have resulted in a technological advancement. Fifth, a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results obtained must have been kept contemporaneously as the work progressed. Justice Spiro also drew upon recent Tax Court jurisprudence—notably Justice Sommerfeldt's definition of a hypothesis in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6, and Chief Justice Rossiter's discussion of trial and error in Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 108—to police the boundary between hypothesis-driven experimentation and empirical trial-and-error.
1.4 The Tax Court of Canada's Final Holding and Cost Disposition

In a judgment initially issued on April 28, 2025, and substituted by an Amended Judgment on May 2, 2025, Justice Spiro dismissed the Appellant's appeals for the 2014 and 2019 taxation years in full. The Court held that the Appellant failed to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that its activities in the 2014 and 2015 taxation years satisfied the five criteria of the Northwest Hydraulic test.

Specifically, Justice Spiro concluded that, in the absence of expert evidence, the Appellant had failed to rebut the Minister's assumption that no scientific or technological uncertainty existed; that its single, overarching "hypothesis" was merely a restatement of the project's objective; that its testing was conducted by trial and error rather than systematic investigation; that it had not shown a technological advance; and that it had not kept a detailed record of hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progressed. The Court awarded the Crown one set of party-and-party costs in accordance with the Tariff. In addition, at the commencement of the hearing the Court granted the Crown's two unopposed motions under section 54 of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure) (the "TCC Rules") to amend its Replies to add further assumptions of fact, with costs fixed at $500 each ($1,000 total) for the two motions (the reasons do not state in whose favour those fixed costs run).
2. Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures
2.1 Subjective versus Objective Technological Uncertainty and the Role of Independent Expert Evidence

The primary legal failure in Vortex Energy occurred at the threshold criterion of the Northwest Hydraulic framework: proving the existence of a genuine technological uncertainty. Justice Spiro emphasized a foundational principle of Canadian SR&ED law that is frequently misunderstood by owner-managed engineering enterprises: technological uncertainty is not assessed on a subjective standard. Whether a specific technical problem—such as managing burner flame harmonics, air inlet pressure ratios, or structural vibration in a 35 million BTU direct-contact water heater—is unknown to the claimant's shareholders or its retained fabrication subcontractors is legally irrelevant. Instead, technological uncertainty must exist objectively at the level of the general state of scientific or engineering knowledge publicly available to competent professionals in the relevant field.

In Vortex Energy, Mr. Bodner testified that dealing with air pressures, burner harmonics, and flame sizing was not a "simple case of routine engineering" for the Appellant's team, noting that they "found out the hard way" that scaling to a larger flame induced severe harmonic disturbances and vessel leakage. However, lay testimony from a corporate shareholder describing operational difficulties does not establish that standard fluid dynamics, combustion engineering, or thermo-acoustic design principles were incapable of predicting or resolving those issues.

Justice Spiro highlighted the complete absence of admissible expert evidence demonstrating that the technical obstacles encountered by the Appellant transcended routine engineering. Where a claimant's internal personnel lack formal scientific or advanced engineering credentials—or where the boundary between complex commercial design and true scientific uncertainty is contested—independent expert testimony is frequently decisive in establishing the baseline state of technology. In Vortex Energy, the Appellant chose not to lead any expert evidence; the Court excluded as inadmissible hearsay Mr. Bodner's account of a subcontractor's view that the required heat output could not be achieved with the available volume, and observed that the Appellant's written argument, by relying on evidence excluded at trial, reflected an impermissible attempt to put expert evidence in "through the back door". Quoting the Code of Conduct for Expert Witnesses in Schedule III to the TCC Rules, Justice Spiro underscored that an expert witness has an overriding duty to assist the Court impartially, must be independent and objective, and must not be an advocate for a party, whereas the evidence of a witness with an interest in the outcome, such as Mr. Bodner, is considerably less credible and less reliable. Without objective expert validation establishing why standard thermal and mechanical engineering equations failed to resolve the burner harmonic phenomena, the Appellant's threshold claim of technological uncertainty collapsed.
2.2 The Fatal Dichotomy Between Intuitive Trial-and-Error and Systematic Investigation

Even where a claimant encounters genuine technical complexity, subsection 248(1) of the ITA mandates that the resolution be pursued through a "systematic investigation or search". Under the second and third criteria of Northwest Hydraulic, this requires the explicit formulation of scientific hypotheses prior to testing, followed by disciplined experimentation and analytical modification of those hypotheses.

Justice Spiro relied on Justice Sommerfeldt's definition in Joel Theatrical Rigging (2017 TCC 6 at para 26) that "a hypothesis is a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial". In a rigorous SR&ED environment, a hypothesis must articulate a testable causal relationship between independent engineering variables (such as burner orifice diameter, stoichiometric air-to-fuel ratio, or packed-bed pressure drop) and dependent performance parameters (such as acoustic pressure oscillation amplitude at specific resonant frequencies), grounded in scientific principles.

The evidentiary record in Vortex Energy revealed an inverse, reactive methodology. Rather than modelling the thermo-acoustic properties of the 10 million BTU and 35 million BTU vessels and formulating hypotheses prior to fabrication, the Appellant built the units, fired the burners, observed destructive vibrations and water leaks ("finding out the hard way"), and subsequently made empirical adjustments to the air inlet system and burner holes until the flame stabilized. Justice Spiro explicitly ruled that this methodology constituted "trial and error". Quoting Chief Justice Rossiter in Canafric Inc. v. The King, the Court reaffirmed that trial and error does not come within the scientific method if used alone because, unlike the systematic investigation required under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, it does not attempt to understand why a particular option did not work and simply moves on to the next option. Trial-and-error seeks solely to make a commercial apparatus function ("what works"), whereas systematic experimental development seeks to uncover the underlying scientific or technological laws governing why a specific technical limitation occurs ("why it works").
2.3 Evidentiary Deficiencies in Contemporaneous Documentation and Uncontextualized Testing Logs

The fifth criterion of the Northwest Hydraulic test requires the claimant to maintain a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results obtained as the work progresses. In Vortex Energy, the Appellant relied on the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada (1998) for the proposition that a lack of documentation is not necessarily fatal; RIS-Christie holds that documentary evidence revealing the logical progression between tests is the only sure way to establish systematic research, but that a court may still infer it where the taxpayer offers a plausible explanation for missing records (such as their accidental destruction) or where the research is shown to have led to a technological advancement, and Justice Spiro found that the Appellant had established neither, since records of failed tests were simply not kept and no technological advance was proven.

In Vortex Energy, the Appellant did not suffer from a complete absence of paper; rather, it suffered from a fatal deficiency in the substantive nature of its records. During his examination-in-chief and the Court's questioning in a voir dire on the admissibility of Tab 100 (Exhibit A-12), Mr. Bodner was asked about his handwritten notes of an April 8, 2014 heating test in Mr. Bazley's farm shop (page 502) and about a June 27, 2014 report by Luc Mandeville on tests of unit no. 1 run on June 25, 2014 (pages 483 to 486, including what Mr. Bodner called the "conclusion on test 46" at the bottom of page 485), and he was unable to show where the theories being tested or the relevant variables were recorded, conceding: "You don't see it. This is just notes of those tests." When asked about page 502 by his own counsel, Mr. Bodner described it as "just some sketch notes that I made on testing our mixing cones for the burner". Similarly, when the Court asked where the record showed that a test had been designed to minimize the size and shape of the flame to eliminate the harmonics, Mr. Bodner conceded, "It doesn't say that," pointing only to the "conclusion on test 46" at the bottom of page 485.

Justice Spiro found that the Appellant had not demonstrated, for any test or series of tests performed in its 2014 or 2015 taxation years, that it recorded the formulation of a hypothesis, the testing of that hypothesis, and its modification in light of the results; there were no records of the tests leading to the destruction of unit number 1 (pressures, temperatures, or the frequency and source of the vibrations) because, by Mr. Bodner's own admission, records of failed experiments were not kept. Uncontextualized shop logs, raw temperature or pressure readouts, and undated field notes recorded during equipment commissioning at a cattle farm only prove that commercial testing occurred; they do not prove that SR&ED occurred. Furthermore, when Mr. Bodner referred during the voir dire to "books and books" of notes at home that had formed part of the Appellant's SR&ED submission, Justice Spiro redirected him to the document actually tendered ("I don't really care what was part of the submission to CRA"); those notes were never put into evidence, and the Court decided the appeals only on the evidence before it at trial.
2.4 Subcontractor Governance, Commercial Fabrication Overlap, and Procedural Missteps

A secondary layer of vulnerability in Vortex Energy involved the work performed by contractors and the commercial character of the units: the Appellant admitted the Minister's assumptions that the contractor hired to modify the water spray nozzles and the computer programming contractor hired to supply the automation software had sufficient experience and expertise for those tasks, and units number 2 and 3 were still being operated commercially alongside fracking crews at the time of the hearing. In the oilfield services industry, building full-scale mobile units (such as the two 10 million BTU heaters and the 35 million BTU heater) involves substantial expenditures on structural steel, welding, standard plumbing, trailer mounting, and third-party subcontractor labour. Under the ITA, arm's-length Canadian subcontractor expenditures are eligible at an 80% inclusion rate only to the extent that the subcontractor performs work directly undertaken on behalf of the claimant that satisfies the statutory definition of SR&ED, or eligible support work under paragraph (d) of subsection 248(1) that is commensurate with the needs of, and directly in support of, the experimental development.

The Court did not decide the appeals on the basis of the commercial production exclusion or any failure to segregate subcontractor costs; rather, the admitted sufficiency of the contractors' expertise supported the Minister's assumption that no technological uncertainty existed, and the appeals failed because the Appellant did not satisfy the Northwest Hydraulic criteria. On the procedural side, at the commencement of the hearing the Crown brought two unopposed motions under section 54 of the TCC Rules to amend its Replies to add assumptions that there was no technological uncertainty, no hypotheses, no systematic investigation, and no purpose of achieving a technological advancement, which the Court granted with costs fixed at $500 for each; Schedules A and B to Justice Spiro's reasons do not concern these motions but reproduce pages 502, 483 to 486, and 513 of the Appellant's test notes (Tab 100, Exhibit A-12).
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table synthesizes the statutory and jurisprudential requirements governing Canadian SR&ED claims, maps them directly against the evidentiary and legal failures identified by Justice Spiro in Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King (2025 TCC 63), and articulates the governing standard of proof required to withstand Tax Court scrutiny.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure in Vortex Energy (2025 TCC 63)
Tax Court Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Expectation

cells: 1. Technological Risk or Uncertainty (Criterion 1 of Northwest Hydraulic)
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1) ("SR&ED" para. (c)); Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen; CW Agencies Inc. v. The Queen.

Pleaded that it "did not know" how its engineering guidelines should address extreme exterior and water temperature variations and a heating chamber likely 60% smaller than existing technology (a subjective standard), and relied on the testimony of Mr. Bodner, an interested shareholder who is not a professional engineer, regarding burner flame harmonics, air pressures, and the catastrophic failure of Unit 1. Failed to call an independent expert witness to prove these issues exceeded routine thermal/mechanical engineering.

Objective Standard on a Balance of Probabilities: Uncertainty must exist relative to the publicly accessible state of scientific/engineering knowledge, not the claimant's internal skill ceiling. Where internal staff lack advanced credentials, independent expert testimony compliant with Schedule III of the TCC Rules is critical.
2. Formulation of Scientific Hypotheses (Criterion 2 of Northwest Hydraulic)
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic; Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6 at para. 26).

Pleaded only a single, overarching "hypothesis" (that a new set of engineering guidelines combined with software-based controls could result in a working mobile direct-fired heater), which the Court held was a restatement of the project's objective, incapable of being tested and "too vague"; no particular hypothesis preceded each test. Discovered harmonic vibration and structural leaking reactively ("found out the hard way") during field operation.

Predictive Causal Proposition: A hypothesis must be formulated ex ante as a specific scientific statement to be tested by experiment or analysis. It must define the expected causal mechanism between design parameters and the targeted technological uncertainty.
3. Accordance with the Scientific Method (Criterion 3 of Northwest Hydraulic)
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1) ("systematic investigation or search... by means of experiment or analysis"); Northwest Hydraulic.

Engaged in empirical "trial and error" by iteratively tweaking air inlets and burner hole configurations during field tests at Mr. Bazley's cattle farm until the flame stabilized and rumbles subsided.

Disciplined Systematic Investigation: The claimant must prove a structured cycle of observation, hypothesis formulation, controlled variable testing, quantitative measurement, and analytical deduction. Intuitive or ad-hoc trial-and-error is legally fatal.
4. Technological Advancement (Criterion 4 of Northwest Hydraulic)
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1) ("for the purpose of achieving technological advancement"); Northwest Hydraulic.

Did not prove a technological advance: in the absence of expert evidence from a professional engineer, the Court had no way of knowing whether building the mobile heaters constituted a technological advance, and Mr. Bodner's evidence on that point was considerably less credible and reliable than that of an independent expert.

Advancement of Underlying Technology Base: The process must generate new knowledge that advances the general understanding of technology (even if the commercial product fails), rather than merely optimizing a product using existing engineering techniques.
5. Detailed Contemporaneous Record-Keeping (Criterion 5 of Northwest Hydraulic)
Northwest Hydraulic; RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada (FCA, 1998); CRA Form T661 & Guide T4088.

Produced uncontextualized field test sheets from the cattle farm (e.g., handwritten April 8, 2014 heating-test notes on p. 502, described by the witness as "just some sketch notes"; a June 2014 test report at pp. 483 to 486 containing what the witness called the "conclusion on test 46") that did not record the hypotheses being tested or their modification, while records of failed tests, including those leading to the destruction of Unit 1, were not kept at all.

Verifiable Contemporaneous Audit Trail: Records must be generated as the work progresses (dated, specific, and structured) and must explicitly link the formulated hypotheses, testing parameters, analytical conclusions, and claimed expenditures. Notes referred to as part of the CRA submission but never put into evidence were of no assistance; the Court assessed only the records tendered at trial.
6. Admissibility of Expert Evidence & Pleadings Compliance
TCC Rules, Schedule III (Code of Conduct for Expert Witnesses) and s. 54 (amendment of pleadings); Syrek v. Canada, 2009 FCA 53.

Chose not to lead expert evidence; relied on inadmissible hearsay of a subcontractor's view and, in written argument, on evidence excluded at trial (an impermissible attempt to put expert evidence in "through the back door"). Separately, the Crown's two unopposed motions under s. 54 of the TCC Rules to amend its own Replies were granted with costs fixed ($500 each; Schedules A and B to the reasons merely reproduce the Appellant's test notes).

Strict Independence and Procedural Gatekeeping: Any witness offering opinion evidence beyond factual observation on the state of technology vs. routine engineering must be properly qualified, independent, objective, and compliant with Schedule III.

body.text: The jurisprudential trajectory reinforced by Vortex Energy directly parallels recent administrative shifts by the CRA. In July 2025—merely two months after Justice Spiro's Amended Judgment—the CRA issued a major revision to The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants. The updated Guide institutionalizes a stricter three-step review framework that places heightened scrutiny on dated, project-specific contemporaneous records, financial ledgers linking expenditures to discrete experimental activities, and clear evidentiary delineation between SR&ED work and routine commercial operations. When read alongside Vortex Energy, the legal reality for Canadian claimants is unequivocal: neither the CRA at the administrative review stage nor the Tax Court of Canada at trial will accept retrospective technical narratives on Part 2 of Form T661 (lines 242, 244, and 246) as a substitute for contemporaneous proof of hypothesis-driven experimentation.
4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how Canadian taxpayers and their technical tax advisors can operationalize the holdings of Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King (2025 TCC 63), the following two applied case studies examine engineering projects vulnerable to the exact legal and evidentiary pitfalls that defeated Vortex Energy's appeal. Each case study provides a step-by-step remedial restructuring across project governance, scientific methodology, contemporaneous documentation, and contractual and financial compliance.
4.1 Case Study One: Thermal-Acoustic Instability in High-Capacity Direct-Contact Industrial Fluid Heaters
Baseline Project Context and Legal Vulnerabilities

A Calgary-based oilfield equipment engineering corporation ("Chinook Thermal Corp.") is designing an ultra-compact, trailer-mounted 40 MMBTU/hr submerged-combustion direct-contact water heater for cold-weather completions in the Montney formation. To comply with highway axle-weight and dimensional limits while tripling thermal density over legacy 12 MMBTU/hr units, Chinook shrinks the combustion chamber volume by 55% and increases the forced-draft blower static pressure. During initial prototype firing at a rural test yard, the unit experiences violent thermo-acoustic pressure oscillations ("combustor rumble"), causing flame blow-off and cracking the stainless-steel packed-bed support grid. Under its legacy practices—identical to the fatal posture in Vortex Energy—Chinook's shop manager and an external welding subcontractor begin cutting and re-welding air inlet baffles and drilling additional burner ports by trial-and-error, recording only exhaust stack temperatures and fuel flow rates on clipboard tally sheets. If audited or litigated in this state, Chinook's SR&ED claim will be disallowed in full for failing Criteria 1, 2, 3, and 5 of Northwest Hydraulic.
Step 1: Project Governance and Establishing Objective Technological Uncertainty

To satisfy Justice Spiro's mandate that technological uncertainty be proven on an objective standard rather than subjective unfamiliarity, Chinook must immediately halt ad-hoc shop modifications and establish a formal SR&ED Project Charter overseen by a qualified Professional Engineer (P.Eng.) with expertise in combustion dynamics, or retain an independent academic or industry combustion specialist. Prior to formulating experiments, the supervising engineer documents a formal "State of Technology Baseline Report" citing standard thermal engineering references (such as ASHRAE, Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook, and ASME burner design codes) to demonstrate why routine engineering solutions—such as installing standard Helmholtz resonators, quarter-wave tubes, or enlarging the firebox—are physically precluded by the system-level spatial constraint of the highway trailer envelope and the multiphase back-pressure generated by the cascading water curtain above the combustion zone.

Rather than claiming the entire mobile water heater as an SR&ED project, Chinook isolates the core technological uncertainty: whether thermo-acoustic coupling between unsteady heat release fluctuations (q′) and acoustic pressure waves (p′) can be attenuated below structural fatigue thresholds (p′ < 2 kPa RMS) within a high-energy-density (> 5 MW/m³) submerged-contact combustion chamber operating against variable two-phase hydraulic counter-pressure, without increasing chamber volume or exceeding emission limits. By having an independent P.Eng. or university thermodynamics researcher review and sign off on this baseline uncertainty analysis contemporaneously, Chinook creates a robust foundation for admissible expert testimony compliant with Schedule III of the TCC Rules should the claim ever proceed to the Tax Court.
Step 2: Restructuring Trial-and-Error into Hypothesis-Driven Experimentation

To overcome Justice Spiro's rejection of empirical trial-and-error and satisfy Joel Theatrical Rigging, Chinook replaces reactive baffle welding with a structured Design of Experiments (DoE) governed by explicit mathematical hypotheses. The engineering team models the thermo-acoustic instability using the Rayleigh Criterion, which states that acoustic energy grows when the integral of the product of pressure oscillation and unsteady heat release rate over an acoustic cycle exceeds the system's acoustic damping losses: ∫₀ᵀ p′(t) q′(t) dt > ∫₀ᵀ L(t) dt, where T is the period of the acoustic cycle and L(t) the rate of acoustic energy dissipation.

Based on this physical law, Chinook formulates Hypothesis 1.1 ex ante: introducing a staged, radially asymmetric swirl-vane air injection geometry with a swirl number S = 0.6–0.8 and staggered fuel orifice pitch will decouple the convective time delay (τ) of the fuel-air mixture from the fundamental longitudinal acoustic mode (f₁ ≈ 95 Hz) of the shortened combustion chamber, shifting the phase angle between p′ and q′ into the damping regime (90° < θ < 270°) across hydraulic liquid-to-gas mass ratios (L/G) from 0.5 to 2.5.

Instead of conducting uninstrumented field tweaks at a farm, Chinook fabricates four modular, instrumented burner nozzles corresponding to discrete swirl numbers (S = 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0). Each test run systematically controls independent variables (air-fuel stoichiometric ratio, water flow rate, inlet air temperature) while measuring dependent acoustic and thermal parameters using high-frequency piezoelectric pressure transducers sampling at 20 kHz, optical chemiluminescence sensors to measure phase, and accelerometers mounted on the vessel wall. When Test Series 1 reveals that S = 0.8 suppresses the fundamental mode but excites a secondary transverse mode at 410 Hz when cold water flow exceeds 120 m³/h due to rapid steam condensation shock at the packing interface, the team analytically falsifies Hypothesis 1.1 for high L/G ratios and formulates Hypothesis 1.2 addressing two-phase boundary layer acoustic impedance. This iterative loop proves strict adherence to the scientific method under Criterion 3 of Northwest Hydraulic.
Step 3: Contemporaneous Documentation Architecture Under the ALCOA+ Standard

To avoid the evidentiary collapse seen in Mr. Bodner's testimony and voir dire questioning over "test 46" and page 502, Chinook implements a mandatory ALCOA+ documentation protocol (Attributable, Legible, Contemporaneous, Original, Accurate, plus Complete, Consistent, Enduring, and Available). Every test run is logged in an immutable digital engineering repository prior to ignition. Each record is time-stamped, signed by the supervising engineer, and links the specific hypothesis tested, the independent variable settings, the raw sensor data attachments, a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) spectral analysis comparing predicted versus actual acoustic amplitude, and the resulting scientific conclusion driving the next hypothesis iteration. Simultaneously, engineering staff and shop technicians log hours daily against specific SR&ED Hypothesis Codes rather than a generic commercial job code, directly satisfying the CRA's July 2025 Review Guide expectations.
Step 4: Contractual and Financial Restructuring for Subcontractors and Prototypes

When Chinook engages an arm's-length Canadian machine shop to fabricate the modular experimental swirl nozzles, the contract is structured with a dedicated SR&ED Statement of Work (SOW). The SOW explicitly stipulates that the work is performed on behalf of Chinook to fabricate non-commercial experimental test components according to Hypothesis 1.1 specifications, and that all intellectual property vests exclusively in Chinook. Commercial welding on the trailer chassis, water tanks, and exterior piping is billed under a separate commercial Purchase Order and excluded from Form T661. Furthermore, because the 40 MMBTU/hr heater is intended for eventual commercial deployment or sale (similar to Units 2 and 3, which were still being operated commercially at the time of the hearing in Vortex Energy), Chinook does not claim the entire cost of the vessel as "materials consumed or transformed". Instead, Chinook claims only the cost of the sacrificial experimental burner inserts and packing grids destroyed during destructive thermo-acoustic testing, alongside the direct labour hours spent executing the experimental test runs.

Subjective assertion by shareholder that burner harmonics were not "routine engineering".

Reactive trial-and-error modification of air inlets and burner holes after vessel leaked.
Ex ante Rayleigh Criterion mathematical modelling and controlled DoE testing discrete swirl numbers (S = 0.4–1.0).
Technical Records
Disorganized test notes that did not record the hypotheses tested ("just some sketch notes" on p. 502 from the April 8, 2014 farm-shop test; "test 46" on p. 485).

body.text: 4.2 Case Study Two: Multi-Phase Slurry Pumping and Cavitation Suppression in Mineral Processing Modules
Baseline Project Context and Legal Vulnerabilities

An Ontario-based industrial process equipment manufacturer ("Laurentian Hydro-Transport Inc.") contracts with a Canadian mining operator to supply a high-pressure, modular hydro-transport pumping system capable of pumping high-viscosity, abrasive magnetite-tailings paste (72% solids by weight) using entrained micro-bubbles for drag reduction. During commissioning of the first full-scale skid, the entrained gas coalesces inside the centrifugal pump volute, causing severe vapour-gas cavitation, violent harmonic pipeline vibrations, and catastrophic impeller erosion within 48 hours.

Facing commercial delivery penalties, Laurentian's lead mechanical designer and two contracted millwrights spend four months swapping impeller geometries, adjusting variable frequency drive (VFD) speeds, and adding chemical defoamers at the test facility until the pump achieves stable discharge pressure. At year-end, an external SR&ED preparer interviews the designer, drafts a polished Form T661 narrative claiming all four months of shop labour, subcontractor invoices, and the entire cost of the pump skid, and files on a contingency fee basis. Under the principles of Vortex Energy, this claim faces total disallowance: the T661 narrative is a retrospective reconstruction, the shop work is undocumented trial-and-error, the commercial contract poses a contract payment reduction and commercial production exclusion risk, and the lack of independent technical evidence fails to separate routine pump curve matching from experimental development.
Step 1: Contractual Restructuring to Prevent Commercial and Funded Research Disqualification

Before addressing technical documentation, Laurentian must insulate its SR&ED claim from contractual disqualification under subsections 127(9) and 248(1) of the ITA. Under section 127 of the ITA, "contract payments" received from a Canadian customer for SR&ED performed on their behalf reduce qualified SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar. To prevent this reduction and avoid the commercial production exclusion, Laurentian structures its customer agreements into two distinct legal instruments: first, an internal, self-funded R&D program wherein Laurentian retains all technical risk, financial burden, and exclusive intellectual property rights to the multiphase cavitation-suppression technology; and second, a commercial equipment supply contract strictly for the sale of a tangible commercial good (the validated pump skid meeting performance specifications) rather than a service contract to perform engineering R&D. This contractual demarcation preserves Laurentian's entitlement to claim internal SR&ED expenditures incurred in resolving the underlying technological uncertainties.
Step 2: Defining Objective Technological Uncertainty and Systematic Protocol

To satisfy Criteria 1, 2, and 3 of Northwest Hydraulic as interpreted in Vortex Energy, Laurentian's chief metallurgist and fluid dynamicist document why standard affinity laws and Net Positive Suction Head Required (NPSHr) corrections for Bingham plastic slurries fail objectively in a three-phase (solid-liquid-microbubble) non-Newtonian regime. Standard hydraulic engineering predicts that increasing suction pressure suppresses vapour cavitation; however, in Laurentian's regime, elevated suction pressure compresses the drag-reducing micro-bubbles, altering the local apparent viscosity and triggering shear-induced particle-gas coalescence at the impeller leading edge.

To resolve this objective conflict of physical mechanisms, Laurentian formulates Hypothesis 2.1 prior to testing: modifying the impeller blade leading-edge sweep angle (β = 15°–35°) and introducing boundary-layer micro-grooves along the low-pressure suction face will maintain a local Weber number below the critical coalescence threshold across the blade passage: We = ρu²d/σ < We<sub>crit</sub> ≈ 4, where ρ is the slurry density, u the local relative velocity, d the bubble diameter and σ the surface tension.

This geometry is hypothesized to prevent shear-induced gas pocket coalescence while simultaneously maintaining a minimum particle Stokes number (Stk > 1) to deflect abrasive magnetite particles away from the blade surface. Rather than tweaking the commercial unit by trial-and-error until it works, Laurentian constructs an instrumented closed-loop test rig using rapid-prototyped sintered impeller inserts. Each trial systematically varies blade sweep at constant slurry rheology, capturing ultrasonic Doppler velocimetry (UDV) profiles and high-frequency acoustic emission cavitation signatures (100 kHz to 1 MHz) to verify or falsify Hypothesis 2.1.
Step 3: Hybrid Automated Evidence Capture and Executive Certification Compliance

To address the documentation and certification vulnerabilities highlighted in recent SR&ED jurisprudence and administrative guidance, Laurentian implements a hybrid documentation workflow that automatically extracts weekly computational fluid dynamics (CFD) git commits, PLC data logs from the closed-loop slurry rig, and time-stamped engineer annotations into a centralized SR&ED dossier. Crucially, rather than relying on automated AI text generation or a detached third-party consultant to reconstruct the technical story from memory at year-end, Laurentian's lead fluid dynamicist reviews and validates the technical summaries monthly. This ensures that Part 2 of Form T661 (lines 242, 244, and 246) is an authentic, contemporaneous reflection of the systematic investigation written by the personnel who directly performed and supervised the work, preparing them thoroughly for CRA technical review interviews.

Prior to filing within the mandatory 18-month statutory window following the fiscal year-end, Laurentian's Chief Financial Officer confirms the irrevocable overhead calculation election in Part 3, Section A of Form T661, selecting the Prescribed Proxy Amount on line 160 (computed strictly on eligible direct employee salaries and never on contractor costs) rather than the traditional overhead method on line 162. Any external tax preparer fee is properly disclosed in Part 9 of Form T661 using the mandatory billing arrangement code (such as code 1 for contingency fees) and is strictly excluded from qualified SR&ED expenditures, as preparer fees are a prescribed non-eligible expenditure for ITC purposes, though deductible as an ordinary business expense. Finally, the authorized corporate signing officer reviews the technical narrative and underlying contemporaneous test dossier before executing the Part 10 certification on Form T661, ensuring the claim can withstand both a 180-day CRA review and judicial scrutiny before the Tax Court of Canada.
5. Strategic Synthesis and Conclusions

The decision in Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King (2025 TCC 63) serves as a definitive warning to Canadian industrial, manufacturing, and energy-sector claimants that commercial engineering complexity does not equate to statutory eligibility under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Justice Spiro's reasons reinforce three non-negotiable pillars of modern SR&ED compliance and litigation in Canada.

First, technological uncertainty is strictly objective. Claimants cannot rely on the fact that a technical obstacle—such as thermal-acoustic burner vibration or mechanical leakage during equipment scale-up—forced their internal team or subcontractors to learn "the hard way". Where a dispute proceeds to the Tax Court of Canada, establishing that a problem lay beyond the reach of standard procedures and routine engineering requires credible, objective proof of the industry baseline, backed where necessary by independent expert testimony adhering strictly to Schedule III of the TCC Rules.

Second, trial and error, used alone, does not come within the scientific method and cannot substitute for systematic investigation. Modifying physical parameters in the field until a commercial apparatus operates satisfactorily—without ex ante formulation of causal scientific hypotheses and controlled analytical testing—fails Criteria 2 and 3 of the Northwest Hydraulic test.

Third, contemporaneous documentation must capture the intellectual and analytical process, not merely raw operational numbers. As demonstrated by the Court's treatment of the Appellant's test notes (Tab 100), which it found scattered and disorganized and which did not record the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses, raw data sheets devoid of explicit hypotheses and analytical reasoning do not establish a systematic investigation, and notes that are referred to but never put into evidence cannot fill that gap. By embedding hypothesis-driven engineering governance, ALCOA+ documentation standards, and strict contractual and financial segregation between commercial fabrication and experimental development from project inception, Canadian corporations can build defensible, audit-ready SR&ED claims that satisfy both the CRA's July 2025 review framework and the rigorous evidentiary standards of the Tax Court of Canada.

outcome: Appeal dismissed; court found missing contemporaneous records and insufficient evidence of systematic investigation defeated the claim.
